cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-baptism.summary: Two dark rivers, labelled 'Fons Ior' and 'Fons Dan', flow together in a great Y-shape to form the Jordan, filled with fish; at their junction a small naked Christ stands in a red font while a figure pours water over him. A Latin caption beside the river refers to Christ's baptism by John. The drawing follows the medieval belief that the Jordan took its name from two springs, Jor and Dan.
facts: The Girona Beatus was completed on 6 July 975 for an abbot Dominicus, probably at the monastery of Tábara; unusually, its painters are named: 'Ende, woman painter and servant of God', and the monk-priest Emeterius.
With 184 surviving miniatures on 284 leaves, it is described as one of the most richly decorated and best documented of the Beatus commentaries.
cur:manuscripts-girona-beatus-baptism.notes: Commons titles the image 'First bath and baptism of Christ'; it belongs to the commentary on Daniel or associated texts at the end of the manuscript (fol. 189).

cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-adoration-.summary: A great circle, ringed with stars and held by four angels at the corners, is divided into compartments: at the centre, in a medallion, stands the Lamb with a cross; around it the four winged living creatures each hold a book, and between them the twenty-four elders raise their crowns, harps and vials. At the top, labelled 'Thronum', two angels flank the composition. The cosmic wheel turns the vision of heaven's worship into a single radiant diagram.
facts: The Morgan Beatus is the work of the painter-scribe Magius (Maius), who is named in a colophon on fol. 293; it is one of the earliest works of the revived Spanish Apocalypse tradition and of so-called Mozarabic art.
The manuscript has 300 leaves of fine parchment and contains, besides Beatus's Commentary, Jerome's Commentary on Daniel.
cur:manuscripts-morgan-beatus-adoration-.notes: Christ appears as the Lamb. The Commons and Metropolitan Museum sources give this as folio 87 or 97; the folio is not certain.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: The haloed Christ stands between a lectern with an open book and an altar, raising his hand toward the hand of God that reaches from heaven, while a lamb stands beneath. The verse above reads 'Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire … then said I, Lo, I come' — words the Letter to the Hebrews places in the mouth of Christ.
facts: Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:objects-harrach-diptych.summary: Two leaves, each with three arcaded fields, present the four evangelists writing beneath their symbols, then the Nativity — the Child lying in the manger with ox and ass beside the Virgin and Joseph — and the Annunciation, and finally the angel greeting the holy women at the tomb and the Crucifixion. On the cross Christ stands upright and alive between Mary and John, with the lance-bearer and sponge-bearer below and the sun and moon above. The diptych gathers the beginning and the saving end of Christ's earthly life under the witness of the Gospels.
facts: The museum label attributes the diptych to the Court School of Charlemagne around 800, the same milieu that produced the ivory covers of the Lorsch Gospels.
Its six fields combine the four evangelists with four Gospel scenes, so that the writers of the Gospels literally stand above the events they recorded.

Q2344437.summary: In the upper half, Christ rises in radiant light on the mountain (traditionally Mount Tabor) between Moses and Elijah while Peter, James and John shield their eyes. Below, in a dramatic contrast of shadow and gesture, the remaining apostles are unable to heal a possessed boy brought by his family. Raphael's last great painting unites divine glory and human need in a single vision.
facts: It was commissioned by Cardinal Giulio de' Medici (later Pope Clement VII) for Narbonne Cathedral in France, but never left Rome.
Raphael died in April 1520 with the painting essentially complete, and for a few days it stood at the head of his bier in his house in Rome.
Napoleon's forces took it to Paris in 1797; it returned to Rome after 1815.
The two episodes follow one another directly in the Gospels, the healing of the boy occurring as Christ descends the mountain.
